what: CNO Financial sells insurance to middle-income Americans, mostly older ones. Its products are life insurance, supplemental health insurance covering what Medicare does not, long-term care policies and annuities, sold through its own agents and by telephone.
customers: Middle-income Americans, concentrated among those near or past retirement, who buy life, supplemental health and long-term care cover and retirement annuities.
money: Fixed annuities and life insurance policies, plus investment income on the reserves.
Medicare supplement, cancer and critical illness cover and other supplemental products.
Long-term care policies and other products.
moat: Insurance premiums are collected before claims are paid, and the money in between — the float — is invested for the company’s benefit. CNO’s distinctive asset is distribution: reaching middle-income older Americans takes a captive agent force and direct marketing that large insurers have generally found unprofitable to build, which limits competition in this segment.
risks: Only four analysts cover the stock, and their $56.75 average target is just 3% above the current price.
Long-term care insurance is the industry’s most notorious product: policies written decades ago assumed costs and lifespans that proved wrong, and the losses emerged over many years.
Annuity profitability depends on the spread between investment returns and the rates promised to policyholders, which interest rates determine.
Last year’s net margin was 5.1%, which is modest, though insurance margins are hard to read from revenue.
Debt of $1.4B is manageable but the business is sensitive to credit losses in its investment portfolio.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 12.6 times earnings, 4.9 times EV/EBITDA and 6.8 times free cash flow.
Free cash flow of $743.1M on $4.5B of revenue, with cash of $983.5M.
Reaching middle-income older Americans requires distribution that large insurers have not built, which limits competition.
An ageing population increases demand for Medicare supplement and supplemental health cover structurally.
Higher interest rates improve the spread earned on annuity reserves, which helps rather than hurts this business.
watch: Policy sales by product line and the investment spread on annuities. Growth comes from policies written; profitability comes from the spread and from claims experience.
view: CNO serves a customer most insurers have decided is not worth the trouble: the middle-income American near or past retirement, who wants a modest life policy, something to cover what Medicare does not, and a safe place for retirement savings. Reaching those people requires agents who visit them and telephone marketing that converts — distribution that the large insurers have generally found uneconomic to build. That is CNO’s real asset, and it limits competition in the segment more effectively than any product feature.

The economics are the insurance economics: premiums arrive before claims are paid, and the float is invested in the meantime. Higher interest rates help this business rather than hurting it, because the spread between what the investments earn and what is promised to annuity holders widens. That is a useful characteristic to own in a higher-rate world, and it is the opposite of how most financial assets behave.

The product to be careful about is long-term care, which is the insurance industry’s most notorious mistake. Policies written decades ago assumed how long people would live and what care would cost, and both assumptions proved badly wrong. The losses emerged slowly over many years, and several insurers were severely damaged. CNO’s exposure is a modest share of the business, but any long-term care book deserves scrutiny rather than a glance.

At 12.6 times earnings, 4.9 times EV/EBITDA and 6.8 times free cash flow, this is priced as an ordinary life insurer, and the demographic tailwind — an ageing population needing exactly these products — is not obviously in the price. The four analysts seeing 3% of upside suggest nobody expects much, which for a cheap, cash-generative insurer with a defended niche is the kind of neglect that sometimes pays. Policy sales and the annuity spread are the numbers to follow.
bull: An ageing middle-income population keeps buying supplemental health and annuities through distribution competitors will not build, and higher rates widen the investment spread.
bear: Long-term care reserves prove inadequate as they have across the industry, credit losses hit the investment portfolio, and a neglected insurer stays neglected.
